name: Ironpass ThermoKnit Compression Layer
description: A workhorse Circuit-tier compression underlayer in charcoal grey with yellow-ochre flatlock seams — Ironpass's signature industrial palette. Constructed from recycled synthetic stretch-knit with a moisture-wicking inner surface and a mild thermal lining that buffers against factory-floor temperature swings. Fits close without binding, designed to sit comfortably under coveralls or work jackets for twelve-hour shifts. The fabric pills at the elbows and collar after heavy use, which most wearers consider proof of honest work.
functionality: Compression support for back and core during heavy labor; moisture management prevents chafing on long shifts. Basic thermal buffering handles ±15°C variance. Seam channels around shoulder blades allow spinal rig hardware to seat without bunching.
what_it_says: You work a real job and you don't make a fuss about it.
manufacturer: Ironpass Workwear — Tier 2 corponation subsidiary label
story_hooks: Ironpass embeds a passive RFID tag in every unit — officially for inventory, but someone's been querying the network at odd hours.
A union organizer is using the sale of bootleg Ironpass compression layers as a funding mechanism for a strike action.
A worker's compression layer preserved a biometric anomaly log from three weeks ago that contradicts the official accident report.

physical_description.visual_profile: A sleek, form-fitting base layer that hugs the torso and arms without restricting movement. The charcoal grey reads as industrial-utilitarian, with striking yellow-ochre flatlock seams running vertically down the sides and horizontally across the shoulders — creating a visual grid that suggests reinforcement and durability. On-body, it reads as 'prepared for work,' neither aspirational nor neglected.
physical_description.fit: Compression-tight through the core and shoulders, tapering snugly at the wrists and waist. Designed to layer invisibly under heavier garments while maintaining freedom of movement through the shoulders and elbows. No excess fabric bunching; sits like a second skin.
physical_description.primary_material: Recycled synthetic stretch-knit with moisture-wicking properties and thermal lining. Feels dense and technical — not soft, but responsive to body heat.
physical_description.texture: Smooth outer surface with a slight ribbed hand-feel from the knit construction. Inner surface is brushed for moisture management. Flatlock seams create subtle raised edges that catch light. Prone to pilling at high-friction zones (elbows, collar, underarms) after extended wear.
physical_description.color_scheme: Charcoal grey base with yellow-ochre flatlock seams. The seams form a geometric pattern suggesting structural integrity — vertical spine seams, horizontal shoulder reinforcement, side-panel demarcation.
physical_description.closures: None — pulls over the head. Friction-fit at wrists and waist through stretch recovery of the knit.
distinctive_features: Yellow-ochre flatlock seams in signature Ironpass grid pattern
Visible pilling at elbows and collar after 50+ hours of wear — worn as a badge of honest labor
Thermal lining visible at neckline and cuffs in charcoal
Subtle brand tag at left shoulder seam
Moisture-wicking inner surface creates faint sheen under sweat
Slight color fade and micro-tears common in sleeve joints after heavy use
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2–3 boundary. Manufactured by a corpo subsidiary (Tier 2 pricing/availability), but worn by working-class Tier 3 factory and warehouse labor. Affordable, durable, and built to be replaced, not cherished.
physical_description.cultural_context: The uniform of shift workers, assembly-line technicians, warehouse handlers, and maintenance crews across the GLMZ. Wearing one signals honest labor, physical competence, and acceptance of corpo-standardized safety/comfort protocols. Also worn by contractors and freelance haulers who adopt corpo-adjacent aesthetics for legitimacy.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in and worn. Pilling at elbows and collar is expected. Slight discoloration from sweat and industrial dust. Small snags or micro-tears at seams after 100+ hours of shift work. Still functional; replacement happens when seams fail or thermal lining delaminates.
